summary: Catalogs issues that have affected how well Internet Routing Registries work for specifying routing policy, and discusses which are still real problems and which are leftovers that still discourage filtering.

eli5.summary: This looks at why a shared directory of network rules has not worked as well as hoped.

what is an internet routing registry
subtitle: Why Internet Routing Registries never lived up to their promise for routing policy, and which of the old excuses no longer hold.

tldr.problem: Internet Routing Registries (IRRs) were meant to let operators share routing policy and filter on it, but their use for inter-domain filtering has stayed limited for about two decades.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sorts the causes into data accuracy, IRR infrastructure operation, historical BGP limits and historical router limits, and says which are still real and which are outdated.
tldr.outcome: Many historical obstacles are gone, but stale data, slow replication and the lack of resource certification remain real limits.

today: RFC 7682 is an Informational RFC. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What IRRs Are For
sections.content:
Internet Routing Registries record bindings such as an origin AS and a prefix, an AS and its import and export policies, and AS macros (as-set objects in the Routing Policy Specification Language, RPSL). The RFC catalogs what hurt their efficacy over the past two decades.

It stresses that the word IRR is often used as a catch-all for three separate topics: the accuracy of data in the IRR, RPSL itself, and the deployment of derived policy on routers. Separating them shows which problems are historical artifacts and which still exist. The idea goes back to RFC 1787, which called for sharing routing requirements across organizations.
sections.eli5: An IRR is a public notebook where network owners write down who may announce which addresses. People blame the notebook for lots of different problems, so this paper sorts them out.

sections.title: Accuracy and Integrity of the Data
sections.content:
The biggest weakness often cited is that IRR data is out of date or lacks integrity. The RFC attributes this to the absence of a resource certification infrastructure: a relying party cannot cryptographically verify an IRR object, and generally there is no assurance of validity at creation time. It says this is not a weakness of RPSL (RFC 2622) itself.

Incentives are lopsided. Customers have a strong reason to add new route objects when an ISP builds filters from the IRR, but little reason to remove old ones, since stale objects with a wrong origin AS are simply ignored by filter generation.

Third parties also cannot remove stale data, because under RPSL only the maintainer named in mnt-by may change an object. The auth-override mechanism of RFC 2725 would have allowed it, but the RFC says it is unclear it was ever implemented or deployed. Finally, given a prefix it is usually impossible to tell which IRR is authoritative, and queries go over unencrypted TCP port 43.
sections.eli5: Anyone can write a note on the board, but only the writer can erase it, and people forget to erase. Nobody can check that a note is true, so old wrong notes pile up.

sections.title: Replication and Policy Updates
sections.content:
Several IRRs use a Near-Real-Time Mirroring (NRTM) protocol to copy each other. The RFC notes it has no way to validate the mirrored copy, uses no security mechanisms, and is generally polled every 5 to 10 minutes. Other providers fetch flat files by FTP that are exported at intervals of typically 2 to 24 hours, and providers typically use a 24-hour cycle.

An ISP fetches a customer's IRR objects, builds a new vendor-dependent policy, compares it with the existing one, and uploads it to routers only if it changed. Because of the 24-hour cycle, a customer who suddenly needs a new prefix announced may have to call the ISP's Network Operations Center, which can often push the change in as little as 5 minutes.

The RFC also says RFC 2769 tried to offer more methodical replication, and suspects it failed to gain traction because it relied on RFC 2725.
sections.eli5: Copies of the board are refreshed only once in a while, sometimes once a day. If you need a change quickly you have to phone someone.

sections.title: Historical BGP and Router Limits
sections.content:
In the past, applying a new BGP policy often meant bouncing the interface or clearing the eBGP session, which disrupted forwarding and was usually done in a maintenance window. BGP soft-reconfiguration and the Route Refresh capability (RFC 2918) let a new policy take effect without resetting the session.

Routers in the mid 1990s rarely supported incrementally updatable prefix filters, so a whole list had to be rewritten, which commonly leaked routes. Routers also had very limited NVRAM, and slow writes could cause lost keep-alives. The RFC says these limits are largely resolved, though configuration growth in some large networks still poses challenges.

Configuration was historically pushed with vendor CLI over telnet or SSH, fetched by TFTP, FTP or SCP. More recently NETCONF (RFC 6241) can be used, but the XML is still vendor dependent.
sections.eli5: Long ago, changing a router's rules meant rewriting the whole list and briefly cutting the connection. Newer routers can change one line at a time without hanging up.

sections.title: Summary and Security
sections.content:
The RFC concludes that many problems that stifled IRR deployment are now historical, but real considerations remain. Without an operationally deployed resource certification framework that ties policy to resource holders, there is a fundamental limitation. The RPKI can sign Route Origin Authorizations, the equivalent of IRR route objects, but the text says it is unclear whether it will be extended to other IRR objects such as aut-num.

On security, the central concern is that an IRR operator can remotely influence an external consumer's routing, for example through burdensome or crafted policy statements. Operators may want to be circumspect about ingesting content from external parties, and a resource certification framework should address authorization of IRR statements.
sections.eli5: Many old problems are fixed, but the biggest one is still there: there is no way to prove who owns what. Until that is solved, people should be careful about trusting what is on the board.
